newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Sharp jump in Irish inflation seen likely.
newsitem.headline: Sharp jump in Irish inflation seen likely.

text.p: Ireland's official economic figures, published on Thursday, imply a sharp jump in inflation in the second half of 1997, economists said.

Continued pressure on the Irish pound will lead to import-led inflationary pressures which may push the consumer price index as high as three percent in the latter part of the year, Riada economist Dan McLaughlin told Reuters.
"Implicit in the government figures is that we will begin to see a much more rapid feed-through of the punt's fall against sterling into inflation, that is clear from their figures," McLaughlin said.
In an annual economic review and outlook, published on Thursday, the Department of Finance forecast 1997 inflation at two percent on average.

"The figure obviously anticipates a significant uptick in inflation in the second half of the year with significant pressure coming from the currency," Bank of Ireland Group Treasury economist Colin Hunt said, noting that inflation in the first half of the year averaged just 1.5 percent.

"Inflation has been flat at 1.5 percent in the first half and if it is to average 2.5 percent on the year, I would not be surprised if, implicitly, the authorities have inflation up around 3.0 percent towards the end of the year," McLaughlin said.

McLaughlin said if sterling stays above three marks, which he expected it would for quite some time, then the sterling/Irish pound exchange rate was likely to remain in the 88-89 pence sterling range ".. with a danger that we will slip below 88 pence".
The Irish pound dipped as low as 87.50 pence stg on Wednesday before recovering to close at 88 pence.
It was trading at 0.8840 stg and 2.7030 marks by mid-morning on Thursday.
"This is obviously significant if you remember that last year we were trading at 1.04 pence stg so we have fallen by 15 percent," McLaughlin said.
Bank of Ireland's Hunt thinks that while sterling is overvalued it could still go higher.

"There is a pinching movement going on, with a weak mark on the basis that the euro is not going to be the most credible currency in the face of the earth, coinciding with the British economy rocketing along in terms of consumer spending."
"Consequently the thought of higher rates in the UK is attracting in overseas funds, so while the currency is overvalued, I think it still has the potential to go a bit higher," he said.
"But when it turns it may turn in style," Hunt warned.

Bloxham economist Alan McQuaid said he did not see sterling weakening enough to ease the Irish authorities' exchange rate dilemma -- their hands are tied due to the weak sterling/Irish pound rate combining with a worryingly high mark/Irish rate within the ERM grid.
The punt is more than 12 percent higher than the weakest currency in the ERM grid, the French franc, fanning fears that it could breach its 15 percent restriction.

On the growth front the review forecast continued buoyancy within the Irish economy revising its gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecast up to 7.4 percent and gross national product (GNP) up to 6.5 percent in 1997.

"They have revised up their growth forecasts to more realistic levels but I think they still err on the side of caution," McLaughlin said. "We are going for growth on 8.0 percent for GDP and 7.0 percent for GNP."
The review expected employment to show an increase of more than 50,000 jobs in 1997, while average unemployment was seen falling by 10,000.
